extracted.intended_audience: general public, researchers and readers interested in aviation safety, corporate governance, and the Boeing 737 MAX incidents
extracted.subtask_description: A compiled, encyclopedic summary of stakeholders' reactions (industry, regulators, pilots, unions, passengers, consumer advocates, analysts) to the Boeing 737 MAX crashes and subsequent global groundings, including criticisms, demands, and proposed reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure safety before return-to-service
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators and Boeing must ensure safety comes first and take as much time as needed before clearing the MAX to return to commercial service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAA Administrator and lawmakers said FAA should take as much time as it needs to ensure safety comes first; criticisms arose that Boeing provided overly optimistic return-to-service timelines such as 'in the coming weeks' which were outdated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper classification of safety‑critical systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that affect flight safety (e.g., MCAS) must be correctly classified as 'safety critical' so they receive appropriate oversight and documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House Committee findings criticized Boeing's not classifying MCAS as 'safety critical' as part of efforts to avoid regulatory oversight; this classification affected whether regulators and pilots were informed and what certification scrutiny applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and disclosure of records and communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing and regulators should disclose relevant internal communications, test data, and records to investigators, regulators and public oversight bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Boeing turning over Forkner's messages, the House Transportation Committee demanding documents, and FlyersRights suing the FAA for access to records; lack of timely disclosure was widely criticized as a 'culture of concealment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and thorough regulatory review
rubrics_metrics.description: National aviation authorities (FAA, EASA, Transport Canada, etc.) should conduct independent assessments and not rely solely on another authority's decision when public safety is at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Airlines, consumer advocates, and some governments called for independent reviews; Airbus contrasted EASA's 'purely safety oriented' mandate with FAA. Calls that Canada and others should not simply follow FAA decisions were made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate pilot training, including simulator training where warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots must receive sufficient, transparent training on all aircraft systems and failure modes; simulator training should be required if necessary to ensure safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot unions and FlyersRights argued for simulator training requirements; complaints arose that pilots were not informed about MCAS and that training materials omitted critical system descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full and accurate documentation in manuals and training materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Aircraft flight manuals, bulletins and training materials must fully describe systems that affect handling so crews can recognize and respond to failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism focused on Boeing's omission of MCAS from pilot documentation and removal of MCAS references from draft AD to focus crews on runaway stabilizer recognition; pilots said they deserve to know what is on their airplanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust software development and testing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Software that affects flight control must be developed with rigorous practices, oversight, and realistic testing to eliminate unintended activations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boeing reported hundreds of test flights with updated MCAS software; reporting of test anomalies (e.g., Wired's report of altitude changes) and criticism of outsourcing and contractor use led to calls for better software development oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive, realistic flight testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Updated software and fixes must undergo extensive, realistic flight testing that demonstrates resolution of failure modes without anomalous behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boeing cited 96 then ~500 test flights; critics noted some test flights involved multiple altitude changes and questioned adequacy and realism of testing prior to certifying fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize safety over production and profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate decision‑making should prioritize passenger safety above production targets, delivery schedules, or profit motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers and commentators accused Boeing of decisions suggesting profit took priority over safety; executives were criticized for pressuring certification timelines and limiting safety testing to speed approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger engineering oversight and independent reporting lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineering staff should have reporting structures that protect safety concerns from commercial pressure; engineers should report to chief engineers and safety groups independent of business management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following reviews, Boeing strengthened engineering oversight so thousands of engineers report to chief engineers; a new safety group and board committee reporting lines were recommended to avoid business pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board and executive accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate governance should hold executives accountable for safety lapses; leadership changes and board reforms may be required after major safety failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal of CEO Dennis Muilenburg and other leadership changes were cited; critics argued for replacing top leaders and reconstituting boards where necessary; overboarding of new chair was also criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and act on whistleblower reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies and regulators must take whistleblower reports seriously, protect whistleblowers from retaliation, and investigate reported safety concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Former employees reported pressure to speed certification and unsafe conditions; whistleblowers like Ed Pierson raised plant safety and quality concerns; calls for protections and investigations followed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit regulatory delegation to industry where conflicts exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators should be cautious in delegating certification authority to manufacturers (e.g., ODA program) because of conflict-of-interest risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics blamed FAA for delegating too much authority to industry and for letting manufacturers influence certification; calls for review of delegation policies ensued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, non‑contradictory public communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements by companies and executives should be consistent, accept responsibility where appropriate, and avoid misleading stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Muilenburg's public communications were criticized as contradictory and unconvincing; observers said Boeing should not deflect blame onto pilots and should answer tough questions honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and remediation for affected airlines and passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers should compensate airlines for disruptions and consider remedies for passengers and victims' families where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most airlines sought compensation for disruption; airlines altered orders and routes; legal and financial consequences (lawsuits, claims) were discussed including classification of crash victims as 'crime victims' in a Texas ruling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent, transparent accident investigation and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident investigations should be independent and aim to identify root causes so the industry can learn and prevent recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations by NTSB, Ethiopian bureau, and congressional committees highlighted multiple contributory causes; commentators emphasized learning from accidents rather than assigning blame only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human factors and clear pilot cues for failure modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and certification must account for human factors so that pilot cues for automated systems/failures are appropriate and distinguishable from other failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony (e.g., Dr. Mica Endsley) noted that MCAS-triggered cues differ significantly from runaway stabilizer cues, complicating pilot response; recommendations included re-examining cockpit design and pilot training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accurate maintenance records and integrity of operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Airlines and maintenance organizations must keep truthful maintenance records and avoid practices that could compromise safety or indicate corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations (e.g., Ethiopian ex-chief engineer) that maintenance records were altered raised concerns about systemic problems and led to calls for independent scrutiny and asylum requests tied to alleged corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid outsourcing critical safety work without sufficient oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Outsourcing of critical development (software, systems) should not be done without strict oversight and assurance of contractor qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism that Boeing outsourced software work to lower‑paid contractors (though not directly MCAS/AoA disagree alert work) raised concerns about quality control and management pressure limiting changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not promise premature return-to-service timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should avoid giving optimistic short timelines for fixes or return-to-service that may be wrong and undermine trust when revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boeing provided several return-to-service timelines such as 'in the coming weeks' that later proved outdated, contributing to criticism about credibility and communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore public confidence through information and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: To regain passenger trust, produce clear information packages, communicate safety steps, and use credible endorsements and visible transparency measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals included Boeing preparing information packages for travelers, public ad campaigns, video capsules featuring chief pilots, airlines reprinting safety cards and coordinated messaging with regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider redesigning flight deck and revising pilot training assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-examine flight deck design and pilot training assumptions—especially if aircraft are expected to be operated by pilots with less training—to ensure safe operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board recommendations included re-examining assumptions around flight deck design and recommending pilot training criteria beyond traditional programs where warranted for new cockpit designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use certification and new accreditation where needed (e.g., SSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop new certification programs and accreditations to address modern systems integration challenges (for example Systems Software Integrator certification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Systems Software Integrator (SSI) certification program through NICET was created in part due to integration issues cited in the 737 MAX response.
